title: Degradation Rehearsal: Scenario Lab & Hypothesis Cookbook
author: Sofia Martinez
content:
Overview

This document is a practical, repeatable playbook for running controlled degradation rehearsals ("what-if" failure injections) against Redwood’s multi-tenant inference platform. The goal is to validate observability, operator workflows, and automated mitigations before customer-impacting incidents occur. It complements the Synthetic Scenario Orchestrator runbook by focusing on hypothesis-driven rehearsal design, measurement postures, and teaching/operator sign-off criteria.

Why run degradation rehearsals?
- Verify that SLOs/SIs and dashboards surface real degradations quickly.
- Confirm that automated routing, fallback, and quota systems behave as intended.
- Validate operator decision paths, runbooks, and escalation templates under realistic load.
- Measure the cost and quality trade-offs of mitigation actions (e.g., model swap, soft-eviction, warmset promotion).

Scope and safe-guards
- Scope: regional multi-tenant stacks, dedicated pools, and edge-prefetch interactions. Not for on-prem private deployments unless explicitly permitted by the customer.
- Safety gates: rehearsal must be approved by platform on-call lead and the impacted tenant owners; a kill-switch must be in place (operator CLI + global circuit-breaker) to immediately halt scenario traffic.
- Blast radius policy: default to 2 non-critical tenants or a reserved synthetic tenant unless an escalated rehearsal has explicit business justification.

High-level workflow
1. Hypothesis definition (Pre-mortem): define the scenario and expected measurable outcomes.
2. Lab configuration: wire up synthetic workload cohorts and telemetry endpoints.
3. Dry-run: validate the control plane, kill-switch, and artifacting of traces/logs.
4. Execution: run the degradation scenario for a bounded window (recommended 10–30 minutes).
5. Observation & mitigation: follow the operator decision canvas and mitigations catalog.
6. Postmortem & artifacting: capture timeline, SLO burns, dashboards, and action items.

Section A — Hypothesis Catalog (examples)
Each hypothesis entry below contains: Description, Input knobs, Expected observables, Mitigation playbook, Measurement recipe, Success criteria.

A1. Prefix KV cache shard failure
- Description: One KV cache shard becomes unavailable leading to elevated cold-start token latencies for affected bundles.
- Input knobs: drop traffic to shard via Istio route rule or simulate disk latency at node.
- Expected observables: 95th/99th token latency increases by 3–5x for affected tenants; model-level prefix cache miss rate spikes to ~100%.
- Mitigation playbook: promote warmset for hot tenants, enable deferred-prefetch hints, and temporarily increase batch size on fallback models.
- Measurement recipe: compare prefix miss rate, first-token latency, token cost delta over a 20-minute window.
- Success criteria: automated warmset promotion reduces 95th token latency by >=30% within 10 minutes; operator manual action path validated.

A2. Regional GPU fleet tail-latency fragmentation
- Description: 25% of GPU nodes in a region experience thermal-induced throttling causing higher per-token latency for long-sequence requests.
- Input knobs: introduce CPU/GPU contention on selected nodes in a canary AZ.
- Expected observables: increased tail latency (p99.9), elevated request retries, tenant-specific SLI burn.
- Mitigation playbook: smart-routing to alternate AZ, model-variant downgrade to quantized variant, temporary routing to dedicated reserved pools.
- Measurement recipe: track latency histograms pre/post routing, model-variant fallback ratio, cost delta.
- Success criteria: routing reduces p99.9 latency to pre-test baseline within allowed SLO window and cost increase is <15% for the remediation window.

A3. Third-party embedding cache TTL regression
- Description: External embedding cache provider returns stale TTLs causing cache churn and increased upstream calls.
- Input knobs: force TTL expiry messages and increase external call latency to 300–800ms.
- Expected observables: embedding call latency increases, token cost increases due to missing embedding caches, alert on embedding error rate.
- Mitigation playbook: switch to local fallback cache, apply backoff, enable circuit-breaker to degrade to cached embeddings.
- Measurement recipe: external call rate/latency, cache hit ratio, embedding call errors, end-to-end request latency.
- Success criteria: local fallback cache reduces external calls by >90% and end-to-end latency impact is <20% after mitigation.

Section B — Lab configuration and templates
Checklist before execution:
- Stakeholder sign-off (platform oncall, SRE lead, impacted tenant owners)
- Test window and rollback window defined in calendar + Runbook ID assigned
- Synthetic cohorts deployed: 2 read-only non-production tenants + 1 production-like synthetic tenant
- Telemetry: dashboards pinned, tracing enabled for involved services, distributed trace sampling set to 100% for the window
- Kill-switch verified and smoke-tested

Config snippets (example Kubernetes job to generate synthetic traffic):
- CLI example:
  PLATFORM_COHORT=degradation-lab-1 \
  TOKEN=synthetic-api-key \
  ./bin/loadgen --target-api https://inference.internal/api/v1/generate --qps 120 --seq-len 1024 --cohort $PLATFORM_COHORT

- Operator kill-switch example (kubectl):
  kubectl annotate svc inference-gateway platform/degradation-test=paused --overwrite

Telemetry dashboard template (fields to pin)
- SLI suite: request_success_rate, p50/p95/p99 token latency, p99.9 tail latency
- Cost signals: tokens_per_request, tokens_per_minute, infra-cost-estimate/hour
- Operator signals: operator_actions, warmset_promotions, routing_changes_count
- External deps: embedding_call_rate, embedding_call_latency, cache_hit_ratio

Section C — Execution playbook (operator facing)
1. Start window: ensure chat ops channel and Zoom are open; notify stakeholders.
2. Run dry-run (2 minutes) to verify traffic reaches synthetic cohort and traces propagate.
3. Toggle injected fault using orchestrator (document the command).
4. Observe dashboards; if SLO burn exceeds pre-approved threshold (default: 5% of monthly burn target), trigger rollback immediately.
5. If mitigation is executed, document time to mitigation and each operator action.
6. End window: remove fault, run warmup for 15 minutes to restore caches and KV state.

Operator decision checklist (quick):
- Can we restore traffic via routing without customer-visible errors?
- Is an automated mitigation (warmset promotion/model-downgrade) available and safe for this tenant?
- If manual intervention required, is the operator runbook step verified?

Section D — Measurement and artifacts to capture
- Timeline CSV: timestamped events (fault_injected, mitigation_started, rollback_initiated, fault_removed)
- Dashboard snapshots: pre, during, and post windows (PNG exports)
- Trace bundles: minimum 100 high-latency traces tagged with scenario id
- Cost delta report: tokens consumed and estimated infra cost delta for window
- Operator log: every command and reasoning captured in the incident channel

Section E — Postmortem template and learning loop
Postmortem sections:
- Purpose and scope of rehearsal
- Hypothesis and result summary (pass/fail)
- Timeline (from injection to final resolution)
- Metrics: SLI delta, cost delta, remediation time-to-effect
- Runbook gaps identified and remediations (owner + ETA)
- Dashboard/alerting changes suggested (owner + ETA)
- Training actions (operator playbook updates, tabletop exercises)

Sign-off criteria
- Platform oncall and SRE lead accept postmortem with action items assigned
- Runbook updates merged and small-playbook exercises scheduled within two weeks
- Dashboard/alert tuning changes deployed to staging and validated in next rehearsal

Section F — Implementation notes and automation ideas
- Parameterize scenario definitions as CRDs so the orchestrator can run them programmatically. Key fields: tolerated_slis, blast_radius, synthetic_cohort_id, telemetry_targets.
- Store rehearsal artifacts in a central S3 bucket with indexed metadata (scenario id, owners, date).
- Auto-generate postmortem drafts from timeline CSV and annotated chat logs to speed sign-off.
- Add a rehearsal-ready flag to platform dashboards so operators can instantly switch context to "rehearsal mode" (auto-adjust alert thresholds and SLO windows).

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: Platform Resilience Team (Platform-SRE)
- Secondary owners: Runtime Ops, Serving Runtime, Observability Guild
- Escalation: Platform oncall -> SRE Lead -> Head of Eng (follow existing oncall escalation policy)

Appendix A — Quick scenario library index
- DRL-001: KV cache shard failure (see A1)
- DRL-002: Regional GPU tail fragmentation (see A2)
- DRL-003: Embedding cache TTL regression (see A3)
- DRL-004: Model-variant incompatibility after quantization rollout (operator swap test)
- DRL-005: Network partition between control plane and compute plane (fail-open fallback validation)
